For example, in Hartum (Estate of) v Loewen, 2007 ABCA 15, amendments were refused when a three-week trial had already been set, experts reports were nearly ready, seven rounds of questioning had taken place and the tremendous amount of work that had taken place all caused real prejudice to the respondent. In Matthison v Bradburn (Estate), 2007 ABCA 173, amendments were refused on the morning of trial in a case which had been commenced ten years earlier and the need for amendments had been apparent many years before. [55] Eon is cited regularly in subsequent decisions from this Court dealing with amendments to pleadings, but there is little to no comment upon whether a presumption of prejudice applies if amendments are sought after a certain time frame. In Brewin v Magyar, 2022 ABKB 729, the Court notes at para 28, that: It will be easier to establish serious prejudice not compensable in costs where the amendments relate to events that occurred long ago, there have been many years of litigation on original pleadings, new amendments fundamentally change the issues, and the amendments will cause further delay such as adjournment of a trial or the need to redo questioning and production of records: Eon Energy, paras 19-28; Jin v Ren, 2014 ABQB 250, paras 31-32; and Precision Forest Industries Ltd v East Prairie Investments Corp, 2018 ABQB 489 (M.), paras 48-49. [56] In Jin, the Court found that amendments were sought at a very late stage in the proceedings, attempted to introduce new representations and allegations, withdrew admissions, and raised defences without having met the prerequisites. In Precision Forest Industries, the Court cites Messenger and concludes that the respondent had met its burden of showing it would suffer non compensable prejudice were the amendments to be allowed when it had been over 14 years since the agreement which formed the basis of the litigation had been signed. The Court notes at para 48 that, “this is a significant period of time and its passage is detrimental to the availability and that quality of evidence”. [57] In Woodbridge Homes Inc v Andrews, 2019 ABQB 585, the Court commented at para 21 that, Amendments proposed even at a very late stage of a civil proceeding are permitted under the general rule, provided that the amendments do not prejudice the opposite party or fall into one of the other exceptions. For example, if all the evidence has already been completed without reference to an issue not raised by the pleadings, prejudice will be virtually inevitable: McDonald v Fellows (1979), 1979 ABCA 224 (CanLII), 17 AR 330 at 336 (Alta CA) [58] Most recently, in RK v GSG, 2024 ABKB 661 at para 7 the Court notes that if an opposing party objects to the proposed amendments, that party bears the onus of proving, on a balance of probabilities, that the amendment falls within one of the exceptions, citing Foda v Capital Health Legion, 2007 ABCA 207 and AARC Society at para 53. [59] The statement of the trial judge in Eon about a presumption of prejudice is an outlier. There is no such presumption. To conclude otherwise would reverse the burden of proof. Other decisions (including those relying upon Eon) confirm that a respondent still bears the burden of proving prejudice, even after a significant passage of time. However, that burden becomes progressively easier to meet the longer the action has been outstanding, and the more steps have been taken to prepare for trial – to the point where it might become “inevitable”. See also “Is Evidence Necessary?” under this rule. 18. Amending Style of Cause After Expiration of Limitation Period In Fiebich v. Ortlieb, 2004 ABCA 256, 2004 CarswellAlta 1132, 354 A.R. 279, 31 Alta. L.R. (4th) 1, O'Leary J.A., speaking for the Court, discussed the amendment of a style of cause after the expiration of the limitation period, and the issue of whether an action is a nullity. In Fiebich, the father of two deceased minors commenced an action in relation to their July 11, 1990 deaths. In the action, he described himself as “the Administrator of the Estates” of the children. In fact, he was not so appointed, and in 1999, the children's mother obtained an order appointing her as administratrix ad litem of the estates “for the purpose of the within action”. The style of cause was amended accordingly. No objection was taken to that amendment. Subsequently, on May 2, 2000, the mother was granted letters of administration in respect of the children's estates, and in August, 2000, she applied to amend the statement of claim by amending the style of cause again to reflect her position as administratrix, and to add to the action claims for loss of future earnings. The Court of Appeal allowed the amendment of the style of cause, and denied the amendment that would have added the claims for loss of future earnings. The latter ruling is set out in the annotation to this Rule entitled “New Action Added after Limitation Period Expires”. As to the amendment of a style of cause after the expiration of a limitation period, O'Leary J.A. said, at pp. 7-9: In Stout Estate v. Golinowski Estate this court held that an action commenced within the limitation period on behalf of an estate by an administrator ad litem appointed for that purpose by a court order was not a nullity but merely an irregularity. It could be cured by amendment of the style of cause outside the limitation period to substitute the duly appointed administrator of the estate. In Stout Estate, claims were advanced by the administrator ad litem on behalf of the estate and on behalf of the deceased's parents for dependency. The defendant applied to strike the statement of claim as disclosing no cause of action on the ground an administrator ad litem cannot, in law, sue on behalf of an estate. Prior to the application being heard, the administrator ad litem was formally appointed administrator of the estate. The administrator then cross-applied to amend the style of cause accordingly. The Chambers judge granted the application to strike and dismissed the application to amend. He held the action was a nullity ab initio and the style of cause could not be amended after expiry of the limitation period. On appeal, the court distinguished the circumstances from cases where an administrator commences an action on behalf of an estate before formal appointment, or where one of the parties is non-existent (deceased, for example) when the action is commenced, which could give rise to characterization of the action as a nullity. Although the appointment of the administrator ad litem to commence the action was improper since an administrator ad litem has been held to lack capacity to commence actions as a representative, the court recognized that the order appointing the administrator ad litem had not been appealed and remained valid until set aside. It was not void ab initio and the action could not, therefore, be characterized as a nullity. The court in Stout Estate relied on an earlier decision of the court, Frank v. Canada (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Affairs) (1987), 88 A.R. 241, 56 Alta. L.R. (2d) 289 (C.A.), the unanimous decision of a five-member panel. There, the court expressly disagreed with the proposition that an order appointing an administrator ad litem to defend an action on behalf of an estate where an administrator had already been appointed should be characterized as void ab initio and a nullity. The court permitted the substitution of the administrator for the administrator ad litem. The court in Stout Estate held at para. 75 that [t]here was a validly, but irregularly appointed, administrator ad litem and a properly constituted action brought on the authority of that appointment. Even if the appointment [of the administrator ad litem] may be validly set aside, neither it, nor the action brought on the basis of it, is a nullity. The court concluded that the principle in Frank should be extended to situations where an action is commenced on behalf of an estate by a court-appointed administrator ad litem. It was held in Stout Estate that neither the order appointing the administrator ad litem nor the claim brought under its authority were nullities. Naming the administrator ad litem as the representative plaintiff was an irregularity. The critical question was whether the irregularity could and should be cured by amendment to substitute the properly appointed general administrator. The order of December 21, 1999 appointing Debby Fiebich administratrix ad litem was for the express purpose of continuing the action on behalf of the infants' estates. The defendants raised no objection to the order and it was never appealed, varied or set aside. It remains valid despite the fact it should not have been made. The claims of the estates were validated by the order. Following the appointment of Debby Fiebich as administratrix ad litem, the status of the claims made on behalf of the estates was as if they had been commenced by her in that capacity within the limitation period. Neither the appointment nor the claims of the estates could be characterized as nullities. For the reasons expressed by this court in Stout Estate and Frank v. King Estate, I conclude that the claims brought on behalf of the infants' estates were not nullities but, rather, curable irregularities. The issue is whether the irregularities can and should be cured by substituting Debby Fiebich in her capacity as administrator after expiry of the limitation period. 19. Misnomer … the proper test to be applied in cases of determining whether or not there has been a misnomer is to ask the question—would a reasonable person reading the document understand that he is the person referred to therein but wrongly named or named under a pseudonym? If so, it is a matter of misnomer and the court will permit amendment of the pleadings in order to properly identify the party. If such is not the case, the rule is that it is not a case of misnomer but simply an attempt to introduce a new party by way of addition or substitution. Brochner v. MacDonald (1988), 56 Alta. L.R. (2d) 72 at 76 (Q.B.). The Court of Appeal has said the same thing: Where an original defendant knows whom the plaintiff intends to sue and that from the statement of claim it is not the one the plaintiff intends to sue and it is clear who the proper defendant is, which is the situation in this instance, then it is a case of misnomer and the amendment should be allowed. J.R. Sheet Metal & Manufacturing Ltd. v. Prairie Wood Products (1980) Ltd. (1986), 42 Alta. L.R. (2d) 378 (C.A.), at 381, per McDermid J.A. In J.R. Sheet Metal & Manufacturing Ltd. v. Prairie Wood Products (1980) Ltd. (1986), 42 Alta. L.R. (2d) 378 (C.A.), Stevenson J.A., as he then was, agreed with the majority's conclusion and, at p. 382, said “the Supreme Court of Canada has approved the application of the test in Davies v. Elsby Bros. Ltd.”. Though his Lordship expressed concerns about the Davies test, he agreed that it correctly set forth the current state of the law on misnomer. The test set forth by Lord Justice Devlin in Davies v. Elsby Brothers Ltd., [1960] 3 All E.R. 672 (C.A.), is set out as follows at p. 676: The test must be: How would a reasonable person receiving the document take it? If, in all the circumstances of the case and looking at the document as a whole, he would say to himself: “Of course it must mean me, but they have got my name wrong”, then there is a case of mere misnomer. If, on the other hand, he would say: “I cannot tell from the document itself whether they mean me or not and I shall have to make inquiries”, then it seems to me that one is getting beyond the realm of misnomer. One of the factors which must operate on the mind of the recipient of a document, and which operates in this case, is whether there is or is not another entity to whom the description on the writ might refer. In Rocklake Enterprises Ltd. v. Timberjack Inc., 2001 ABCA 191, 2001 CarswellAlta 1045, 293 A.R. 124, 94 Alta. L.R. (3d) 257, Côté J.A., speaking for the majority, said, at p. 268: Besides, those authorities which call for an objective test and ask what the reasonable reader of the statement of claim would realize, emphasize that that must be done without further inquiry. … I am not aware of any authority which lets one change a party after the limitation period expires because the other party could have conducted research which would have revealed the error. In Nichwolodoff v. Edmonds, 2001 ABQB 613, 2001 CarswellAlta 954, 291 A.R. 384, 93 Alta. L.R. (3d) 153 (Q.B.), Lefsrud J. gave the following summary of the law regarding amendments in cases of misnomer. At pp. 157-158, his Lordship said: Amendments may be made to a statement of claim despite the expiration of the applicable limitation period if the misnaming of a party was a mere “misnomer” (Ladouceur v. Howarth (1973), 41 D.L.R. (3d) 416 (S.C.C.)). The proper form of analysis for cases of misnomer was set out in Nagy v. Phillips (1996), 137 D.L.R. (4th) 715 (Alta. C.A.). The following questions must be addressed: 1. Is this a case of misnomer according to the test set out in Davies v. Elsby Brothers Ltd.… 2. If so, were the Defendants misled or substantially injured by the misnomer? 3. Did the Plaintiff show due diligence, or a lack of unreasonable delay, in finding out the correct names of the Defendants and applying to amend to substitute them in the Statement of Claim? This last point was also noted by Moen J. in Bell v. Chana, 2006 ABQB 139, 2006 CarswellAlta 882, 403 A.R. 115, 60 Alta. L.R. (4th) 320, at p. 331: In a misnomer case, the judge should not grant an application to substitute a defendant unless “…the applicant has been reasonably diligent to seek to properly identify the desired defendant.” See also the annotations under “Test of Misnomer” and “Correction of Misnomer” under R. 38. 20. Effective Date of Amendment The amendment relates back to the commencement of the action. See Owens v. Calgary Farmer (The), [1927] 3 W.W.R. 62 (Alta. T.D.). The amendments to the statement of claim are effective and take effect from the date the statement of claim was issued. Bernard v. Yurich (1987), 81 A.R. 1 at 11 (Master). In Korte v. Cormie (1996), 36 Alta. L.R. (3d) 431 (C.A.), Madam Justice Hunt, speaking for the court, said, at p. 443: The authorities suggest that an amendment usually dates from the date of the statement of claim… However, where an amendment is permitted that adds a new cause of action, the Court may order that the new cause of action takes effect only from the date of the amendment. 21. Withdrawing Representation Made By Counsel Regarding Claim In Chenen Resources Ltd. v. EnCana Corp., 2006 ABQB 931, 2006 CarswellAlta 2050, 411 A.R. 1, an action was commenced against EnCana by the plaintiff, Chenen Resources alleging breaches of a gas marketing agreement. Counsel for EnCana asked counsel for Chenen if the plaintiff “was going to pursue a claim for damages relating to the exploration and production aspect” of certain business which occurred in November 2004 (described as the CanEnerco business). Counsel for Chenen replied that “I can now confirm that the damages claimed in this action are not with respect to the Exploration and Production aspect of CanEnerco's business. The primary focus of the damages are the other two aspects: namely, marketing and gas storage business.” Wilkins J. held that the words “the primary focus of the damages are the two other aspects” should be “interpreted as a binding representation that Chenen will conduct their case in a particular manner. So categorized, leave of the Court is required for Chenen to withdraw it.” At p. 8, Wilkins J. said: 48 The test for that leave is in my opinion correctly set forth in Edmonton (City) v. Lovat Tunnel Equipment Inc., [2000] A.J. No. 87. In that case, the Court concluded that a representation of counsel was tantamount to an amendment of the plaintiff's proceeding to withdraw a claim. Justice Lee concluded that the test for leave to withdraw in relation to such a representation is the same as for a further amendment of a pleading to reassert that claim. That is, it will be permitted where it can be made without prejudice to the opposite party which cannot be compensated in costs, there is no undue delay; and no limitation defence would be lost to the defendant. 22. Concurrent applications to amend and to strike In Hur v. 726913 Alberta Ltd., 2013 ABQB 208, Mr. Justice Brown said: 27 Where an application for summary judgment is heard concurrently with a cross-application for permission to amend pleadings, the Court must determine the amendment application first before determining the application for summary judgment. (Elbow River Marketing Limited Partnership v. Canada Clean Fuels Inc., 2011 ABCA 258 at para. 3) It appears, from the face of Master Breitkreuz's order, that he followed this procedure, deferring consideration of summary judgment until the state of the pleadings had been determined: he first denied the Plaintiffs' application to amend the Statement of Claim, then summarily dismissed the Plaintiffs' claim against the Defendants. An example of the application of this direction is found in Michael Awad Professional Corp. v. 531845 Alberta Inc., 2015 ABQB 296 (Master). Master Robertson said: 14 Before oral arguments got underway, I drew to the attention of the parties Hur v. 726913 Alberta Ltd., 2013 ABQB 208 at para. 27, where the Court said that where there are cross-applications both for summary judgment and to amend the claim the court must hear and decide the application to amend before considering summary judgment. Also, in Chevalier v. Sunshine Village Corporation, 2011 ABQB 544, the Master allowed an application to amend to be brought before making his decision on an application to strike under Rule 3.68. 15 Accordingly, although the applications were argued together, it is incumbent upon the Court to decide the amendment application before deciding the application to strike. 16 It is not necessary for the defendant to bring a new application to strike; it is possible to deal with the application to strike taking into account the amended pleading, if in fact an amendment is allowed. The Court must simply look at the proposed amended pleading instead of the original one to determine if it discloses a reasonable cause of action. 17 The application is made a little awkward by the fact that on an application to amend, there must be affidavit evidence filed in support to substantiate the need for the amendments. In contrast, on an application to strike under Rule 3.68, the court is required to look only at the pleading and not at evidence. Accordingly, I must consider the evidence that has been filed in support of the application to amend, but then ignore it for the application to strike.

sentences.text: Commentary § 3.65:1 Rule 3.65 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta.
Reg.
Overview In Manson Insulation Products Ltd. v.

Crossroads C & I Distributors, 2011 ABQB 51, 2011 CarswellAlta 108, Justice Poelman said, at paragraphs 42–46: 42 Rule 3.65 gives no substantive guidelines on when amendments not adding parties should be granted.

Apart from formal requirements, it simply states that “the Court may give permission to amend a pleading.” 43 The most analogous former provision is rule 132, which stated as follows: The court may at any stage of the proceedings allow any party to alter or amend his pleadings or other proceedings in such manner and on such terms as may be necessary for the purpose of determining the real question in issue between the parties.
44 The reference to “purpose of determining the real question in issue between the parties” does not appear in rule 3.65.
However, rule 1.2(2)(a) includes that purpose in the overall purpose and intention of the new Alberta Rules of Court.
Thus, rule 3.65 cannot be seen as a change from the approach taken by the courts under the former rule 132.
45 The principles to be applied on amendment applications, established by the authorities under the formal rules, were recently summarized by Wittmann C.J.Q.B.
[in Dow Chemical Canada Inc. v.
Nova Chemicals Corporation 2010 ABQB 524, at paragraphs 20-21] as follows: [20] Generally, any pleading can be amended no matter how careless or late is the party seeking to amend: Balm v.
3512061 Canada Ltd., 2003 ABCA 98, 327 A.R.
149 at para.
This is referred to in Balm as the “classic rule”.
[21] The classic rule is subject to four major exceptions: Canadian Deposit Insurance Corp. v.
Canadian Commercial Bank, 2000 ABQB 440, 269 A.R.
49 at para.
11; Foda v.
Capital Health Region, 2007 ABCA 207 at para.
10; see also C.H.S. v.
Alberta (Director of Child Welfare), 2006 ABQB 528, 403 A.R.
103 at para.

Those exceptions are as follows: 1. the amendment would cause serious prejudice to the opposing party, not compensable in costs; 2. the amendment requested is “hopeless” (an amendment that, if were in the original pleadings, would have been struck); 3. unless permitted by statute, the amendment seeks to add a new party or a new cause of action after the expiry of a limitation period; and 4. there is an element of bad faith associated with the failure to plead the amendment in the first instance.
Therefore, if no exception applies, the pleadings can generally be amended.
46 The principles summarized by Wittmann C.J.Q.B. were not premised on particular words in the old rules.
Rather, they arose from the function of pleadings before our contemporary common law courts.
As stated by Bensler J.
[in Newel Post Developments Ltd. v.

1402801 Alberta Ltd., 2010 ABQB 660 at paragraph 18]: [18] This discretion [to amend pleadings] exists because “pleadings are not a meaningless ritual incantation or medieval superstition; they fulfil the first rule of natural justice, knowledge of the case against one”: Waquan v.
Canada, 2002 ABCA 110, 303 A.R.
43, 2 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 1 at para.
Furthermore, with the Court bound to decide a matter upon the issues pled before it, accurate pleadings are necessary for just decisions.
In Quadrangle Holdings Ltd. v.
Coady, 2012 ABQB 22, 2012 CarswellAlta 86, 531 A.R.

48, Justice McCarthy relied on Manson Insulation Products Ltd., and said, at paragraph 22: Therefore, it appears that under the new rules pleadings can be amended no matter how careless or late is the party seeking to amend.
In Elbow River Marketing Ltd.
Partnership v.
Canada Clean Fuels Inc., 2012 ABQB 277, 2012 CarswellAlta 790, 538 A.R.
L.R.
(5th) 359; reversed 2012 ABCA 328, 2012 CarswellAlta 1914, 539 A.R.
68, 69 Alta.
L.R.
(5th) 22, at paragraphs 19-20, Justice Tilleman followed the law set out above from Ignition Energy Ltd. v.
Direct Energy Marketing Ltd., 2011 ABQB 90, 2011 CarswellAlta 195, and Manson Insulation Products Ltd. v.
Crossroads C & I Distributors, 2011 ABQB 51, 2011 CarswellAlta 108.
In Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. v.
Arcelormittal Tubular Products Roman S.A., 2012 ABQB 679, 2012 CarswellAlta 2257, 549 A.R.
72, 79 Atla.
L.R.
(5th) 1; [affirmed 2013 ABCA 87] Madam Justice Hughes also quoted with approval Whittmann C.J.Q.B. in Dow Chemical Canada Inc. v.
Nova Chemicals Corp., 2010 ABQB 524 at paragraph 36.
Her Ladyship then discussed amendment applications which do not require evidence.

At paragraphs 47-48, her Ladyship said: 47 Amendments which are trivial, such as those that do not seek to impose any liability on new defendants, or those that are purely ancillary, do not require evidence: Balm at paras 9 and 23.
See also Mikisew Cree First Nation v.

Canada, 2002 ABCA 110 at para 26, 303 AR 43 [“Mikisew”] 48 Amendments pleading a new cause of action or claim arising from facts already plead in existing pleadings filed in time, also require little if any evidence.
In Balm, Côté JA observed at para 11: Paragraph 37 in the amended statement of claim is new, and is clearly a new cause of action.
However, though the legal conclusion pleaded is new, the acts alleged in it are not new.
It is trite law that a statement of claim need not name causes of action or draw legal conclusions.
It need only plead facts.

So the plaintiff could merely have sent the original defendants' counsel a letter warning that he would argue at trial that proof of such and such facts already alleged in the statement of claim would constitute the cause of action of mutuality of obligations under law merchant.
See 30 Hals.
Laws 7 (3rd Ed.

At paragraphs 49–51, 53–56, she discussed the evidence necessary for a significant amendment: 49 The leading Alberta case respecting the evidentiary burden and the nature of the evidence required for substantive amendments to pleadings is Balm.
Côté JA summarized the law at paras 25 and 26 as follows: When evidence is needed to support a significant amendment to a pleading, before the limitation period has expired, what evidence is needed?
The Waquan (Mikisew) case, supra, does not address the point (except for some discussion about use of discovery evidence).
I have not found much direct authority on the topic.

(One reason is that England, British Columbia, and the Federal Court of Canada require no evidence at all.) One case says that the test is whether in the evidence filed to support the proposed amendment “facts were alleged from which it could be inferred that” the facts to be pleaded occurred: Wil-Ton Constr. v.
Amerada Minerals Corp.
L.R.
Chief Justice Moore held that the evidence need not be enough to prove the new allegations on a balance of probabilities: Anderson Expl. v.
Pan-Alberta Gas (1998) 224 A.R.
Possibly Kent J. was stating a standard when she called for “more than a scintilla of evidence”, in Firemaster Oilfield Services v.
Safety Boss (Can.) (1993) (June 14 ‘96) J.D.E.
She said that “everyone is in agreement that the threshold is low”: ibid.
The chambers judge here adverted to that standard of proof (in his paras.
Hearsay clearly suffices: Marathon Constr.
(Alta.) v.
Bank of N.S.
R.
The appellants’ factum does not cite any authority which contradicts those propositions.
Of course any admissible evidence will do.
It need not be an affidavit by the party seeking to amend: Sheckter v.
W.
Motor Hotels (Edm.), (1985) 61 A.R.
50 It is clear from the above passage in Balm that the evidentiary standard is very low and that the type of admissible evidence to support new amendments includes hearsay evidence.
51 In CHS v.
Alberta (Director of Child Welfare) 2006 ABQB 528 at para 11, 403 AR 103, aff'd 2006 ABCA 355, 401 A.R.
215, the Court considered the evidence required: Only a modest amount of evidence is needed to support an amendment.

An amendment will only be refused based on an argument that it is “bound to fail on the merits” if it is clear that there is no genuine issue for trial, and the amended claim would not survive a summary judgment application.
These principles are set out in a number of cases, including Mikisew Cree First Nation v.
Canada, 2000 ABQB 899, 86 Alta.
L.R.
375 at para.
7; Rago Millwork & Supplies Co.
Ltd. v.
D.
Woodhouse Construction Ltd.
Alberta (Attorney General), 2004 ABQB 979 at para.11; Balm v.
3512061 Canada Ltd., 2003 ABCA 98, 14 Alta.
L.R.
25; Brar v.
290 at paras.
17-18. … 53 Although only modest evidence need be provided, it must have some foundation in fact.
54 Those opposing the Defendants' proposed amendments assert that amendments must be supported by evidence of sufficient cogency, relying on JAV International Ventures Ltd v.
Halliburton Group Canada Inc, 2008 ABCA 99.
In that case, the respondents sought to admit affidavit evidence in support of their pleading amendments which detailed conversations that had taken place during privileged settlement negotiations.
The issue before the Court was whether the evidentiary foundation supported the Respondents's position that privilege had been waived.

The only comment respecting the evidentiary burden in an amendment to pleadings application is in the first sentence in para 5 which states: In the context of an application to amend the pleadings, the evidentiary burden is “modest”.

At this stage of the proceedings, for purposes of the Respondents' motion to amend the pleadings, the threshold for admissibility is, in our view, prima facie evidence of sufficient cogency that the allegations have some foundation in fact.

[emphasis added] 55 I find the phrase “evidence of specific cogency” in the JAV case applies to the evidentiary foundation to support the Respondent's position the privilege had been waived, and not to the evidentiary burden on an application to amend.
56 The parties opposing the Defendants' proposed amendments introduced evidence that could be found to be contrary to the evidence proffered by the Defendants.
It must be remembered that the purpose of these applications is not to make findings of fact or to finally decide the issues raised in the pleadings.
The evidence submitted in support of the amendments may be contradictory to other evidence submitted.
I need only determine if there is “some” evidence supporting the proposed amendments.

As Côté JA stated in Balm at para 13: It is for that reason that the court will authorize a party to amend his pleadings, even if he has given some examination for discovery answers inconsistent with that proposed amendment: Neogleous v.
Toffolon (No.
The appellants made just that objection here.
They do argue that the claim against 070 and Jonathon is hopeless, but try to do so on the basis of evidence as to lack of damage, especially a cross-examination admission by the plaintiff.
This is not a motion for summary judgment by the plaintiff.
Doubt avails the appellants nothing.
[emphasis in original] In Attila Dogan Construction v.
AMEC Americas Ltd., 2013 ABQB 525, 2013 CarswellAlta 1979, 565 A.R.
1; affirmed 2014 ABCA 74, 2014 CarswellAlta 269, 569 A.R.
308, Chief Justice Wittmann agreed with Hughes J., and said, at paragraph 21: 21 I agree with the proposition set out by Hughes J. in Canadian Natural at para.
53, that, in general, although only modest evidence need be provided, any amendment to add new facts of substance should have some basis in evidence, though the standard may be low.

I further take the view that if the proposed amendment is made to add allegations of undue influence and duress, it should be supported by particulars and a somewhat higher evidentiary standard will apply.

The parties directed me to no authorities that would directly support the proposition that the Court should disregard the evidence that has been brought before it on an amendment application when attempting to determine whether a proposed amendment is hopeless.
It is appropriate, therefore, to briefly consider the evidence that AD has brought in support of this application in considering whether the duress and undue influence claims may proceed.
In RK v.

GSG, 2024 ABKB 661, additional reasons 2024 ABKB 771, Justice Mah gave the following summary of the law relating to the amendment of pleadings: [7] In considering the proposed amendments to the Statement of Claim, I have regard to the following principles established by caselaw: • While the Rules of Court authorize the Court to allow amendments, there is no provision to guide that discretion.

The guidance is provided by the decided cases: AARC Society v Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, 2019 ABCA 125 at para 51. • The common law states that discretion should be exercised generously: Andritz Ltd v Quality Fabricating and Supply Ltd., 2010 ABQB 101 at para 43.

Indeed, the so-called “classic rule” is that “any pleading can be amended no matter how careless or late is the party seeking to amend”: Balm v 3512061 Canada Ltd, 2003 ABCA 98 at para 43. • The rationale for this liberal approach is simple: “pleadings are not a meaningless ritual incantation or medieval superstition…they fulfil the first rule of natural justice, [which is] knowledge of the case against one”: Waquan v Canada, 2002 ABCA 110 at para 85.

Insofar as amendments can help identify key issues of contention and keep matters moving expeditiously through the system, there is a strong presumption in favour of allowing amendments: AARC Society, paras 55-56. • Before granting an amendment application, the Court should consider two separate but equally-weighted interests: the litigation interests of the opposing party, and the public interest in having the matter conclude in a timely manner with as little expenditure of public and private resources as possible: AARC Society, paras 58-62. • If the amendment is merely to add particulars—rather than, for example, a new Defendant or a new cause of action—permission should be readily granted, because the prejudice to the opposing party can be presumed to be limited: Rabbit Hill Recreations Inc v Stelter, 2009 ABQB 329 at para 82. • On the whole, amendments are generally permitted, subject to narrow enumerated objections: Farm Credit Canada v Chan, 2021 ABCA 168 at para 21.

If an opposing party objects to the proposed amendments, that party bears the onus of proving, on a balance of probabilities, that the amendment falls within one of the exceptions: Foda v Capital Health Region, 2007 ABCA 207 at para 10
AARC Society at para 53.

An amendment can be denied if: ◦ The amendment would cause serious prejudice to the opposing party that could not be compensated through enhanced costs - i.e. prejudice arising from the passage of time; ◦ The amendment is “hopeless” – i.e. that it would have been struck out if it had been in the original application; ◦ The amendment seeks to add a new party or a new cause of action after the expiration of the limitations period (unless expressly permitted by statute); or ◦ There is an element of bad faith associated with the failure to include the new information in the original pleading.

[8] Caselaw further illuminates the contours of the above exceptions: • Serious prejudice ◦ Delay is closely connected to prejudice—so any prejudice arising from delay will be assessed on a case-by-case and fact-driven basis.
Delay, in and of itself, does not create prejudice enough to block an application to amend.
Unless there is an expired limitations period, an amendment cannot be barred simply because it is late.

However, the timing of the application relative to the life-cycle of the litigation as a whole is of some relevance: Pace v Economical Mutual Insurance, 2021 ABCA 1 at paras 51-52. ◦ The party asserting prejudice bears the onus of establishing it: Balm at para 43.

The passage of several years between the time when counsel should have been aware of the issue giving rise to the amendment and the actual application creates the automatic presumption of serious prejudice: Eon Energy Ltd v Ferrybank Resources Ltd, 2018 ABCA 243 at paras 26-27

Domenic Construction Ltd v Primewest Capital Corporation, 2019 ABQB 58 at para 69. • “Hopeless” ◦ An amendment application should not be granted where the claim is hopeless, such that the pleading would have been struck if originally pled: McCargar v Metis Nation of Alberta Association, 2017 ABQB 692 at para 7, aff'd 2018 ABCA 144.

A pleading is hopeless only if it is clear and obvious that it contains no triable issue, which is something giving rise to a claim recognized in law: McCargar (QB) at para 19. ◦ The evidentiary threshold to support an amendment application is usually low—but after the close of pleadings, “some” evidence is required to amend: Attila Dogan Construction and Installation Co Inc v AMEC America's Ltd, 2014 ABCA 74 at para 27.

Where the proposed amendment raises allegations of fraud, high-handedness, or malicious conduct, there must be “good ground” or “exceptional circumstances” to permit such amendments. “Significant evidence” is required to prove “good ground”: Canadian Natural Resources Limited v Arcelormitall Tubular Products Roman SA, 2013 ABCA 87 at paras 11-12], quoting Mikisew Cree First Nation v Canada, 2002 ABCA 110.

However, the applicant does not need to adduce enough evidence to show that the amended pleading can be proven at trial, or to meet the test for summary judgement: Attila Dogan at para 26. • Limitations-Barred ◦ An amendment takes retroactive effect going back to the date of the original pleading, as if it had been part of the original pleading all along: PTL Bobcat and Landscape Services Lt. v 1149218 Alberta Ltd, 2013 ABQB 158 at para 32.

Any amendment that would add a new cause of action or a new party outside of the limitations period is barred, apart from statutory exception. ◦ If a cause of action has already been pled within the limitations period, then further particulars about that cause of action can be pled outside the limitations period.
Under these circumstances, there is no resulting prejudice to the other party, who has had knowledge of the claim against them (in broad terms, at least) since the beginning.
However, if the “particulars” go beyond the scope of the original Statement of Claim, there may be a valid limitations defense.

Trying to slip in an improper amendment under the guise of “particulars” is inappropriate: Geophysical Service Incorporated v Plains Midstream Canada ULC, 2021 ABCA 55 at para 5. ◦ When amendments are sought after possible expiry of a limitation period, it is best practice to resolve the limitations issue at the time the amendment application is made.

If the complexity of the facts, or the state of the record, preclude a final decision on the limitations issue, the amendments should be allowed and the Defendants be permitted to plead the limitations defense at trial: Domenic Construction Ltd v Primewest Capital Corp., 2020 ABCA 265 at paras 23-28. • Bad Faith ◦ An amendment can be barred where either the amendment itself, or its timing, shows bad faith: Hur v 726913 Alberta Ltd., 2013 ABQB 208 at paras 83-84.
Bad faith involves an intention to harm the other party, to conceal information relevant to the issues, or to deceive either the other party or the Court.
This requisite intent to harm, deceive, or conceal must form a significant part of the party's overall motivation: CS v MS, 2007 CanLII 20279 (ONSC) at para 17.
The timing of an amendment application cannot, on its own, prove that an amendment is being brought in bad faith: 926 Capital Corp v Petro River Oil Corp, 2016 ABQB 194 at paras 33-37.

The bad faith exception is not intended to punish negligent or careless delay that can be recompensed through costs: Club Industrial Trailers v Paramount Structures, 2022 ABQB 34 at paras 35-36. • Since “relevance is the foundation of pleadings”, relevance (or lack of it) is a ground upon which to deny an amendment: Angus Partnership Inc v Salvation Army (Governing Council), 2014 ABCA 423 at para 8.
Further, amendments to pleadings should clarify and not obfuscate the issues before the Court.

Pleadings, and amendments to pleadings, are to be as brief as possible and are meant to assist in the clarification of the issues before the Court: Devon Canada Corporation v Transcanada Power Services Ltd, 2007 ABQB 479 at para 105.

An allowable amendment must be necessary for determining the real question in issue between the parties, the amendment must be useful in determining the real issues, the amendment must plead material facts, not evidence or argument and any new facts plead must be supported by evidence: Devon Canada at para 106.
[9] Thus, it seems to me from the foregoing review of caselaw that an amendment must also be relevant and necessary (as described above) to be allowable.

Expressed otherwise, that an amendment is “irrelevant or useless” (in terms of assisting with the issues before the Court) is a notional fifth category of exception to the general rule of permitting amendments.
See also: Justice Feth's summary of the law in Mikisew Cree First Nation v.
Alberta, 2024 ABKB 578 at paragraphs 16-18.

At paragraphs 21-22 of that decision, Justice Feth added: [21] Where a cross-application to amend pleadings is brought in response to an application to strike, the general practice is to first determine whether the amendments are granted: United Petroleum Distributors (Calgary) v 548311 Alberta Ltd, 1998 ABCA 121 at para 5, 216 AR 116.
However, the general practice may be varied if the proposed amendments will not change the result: Carbone v McMahon, 2015 ABCA 263 at para 8; Carbone v Burnett, 2019 ABQB 98 at para 38.

[22] The general practice serves to clarify the pleadings before analyzing whether the Statement of Claim establishes a reasonable cause of action, rather than anticipating what the amendments might be.

Overview of the law In Club Industrial Trailers v.

Paramount Structures, 2022 ABQB 34, 2022 CarswellAlta 90, Justice Feth gave the following summary of the law: Principles guiding amendments to pleadings [19] Before or after the close of pleadings, the Court may give permission to amend a pleading: Rule 3.65.

[20] The “classic rule” is that amendments are allowed, no matter how careless or late, unless there is prejudice to the other side and the prejudice cannot be repaired (by costs, consequent amendments, an adjournment or other measures): Balm v 3512061 Canada Ltd, 2003 ABCA 98 at para 43 [Balm]
CHS v Alberta (Director of Child Welfare), 2006 ABQB 528at para 11 [CHS].
[21] The classic rule is a “presumption in favor of allowing amendments”: AARC Society v Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, 2019 ABCA 125 at paras 54, 115.
The Court's discretion is to be exercised generously: Andritz Ltd v Quality Fabricating and Supply Ltd, 2010 ABQB 101 at para 43.
[22] Amendments are therefore generally permitted, subject to “narrow exceptions”: Farm Credit Canada v Chan, 2021 ABCA 168 at para 17 [Farm Credit].

The four established exceptions were confirmed in Domenic Construction Ltd v Primewest Capital Corp, 2020 ABCA 265 at para 20: a. unless permitted by statute, the amendment seeks to add a new party or a new cause of action after the expiry of a limitation period; b. the amendment requested is impermissible, sometimes described as “hopeless” (an amendment that, if it had been in the original pleadings, would have been struck); c. the amendment would cause serious prejudice to the opposing party, not compensable in costs; or d. there is an element of bad faith associated with the failure to plead the amendment in the first instance.
See also: Dow Chemical Canada Inc v Nova Chemicals Corporation, 2010 ABQB 524 at paras 20-21.

[23] The amount of evidence required to justify an amendment is low; the applicant need not demonstrate that the amended pleading can be proven at trial: Attila Dogan Construction and Installation Co Inc v AMEC Americas Limited, 2014 ABCA 74 at paras 24, 26 [Attila].
[24] A “low” or “modest” degree of evidence may justify an amendment to pleadings, even if contradictory evidence is presented: Attila at para 26; Balm at para 29.

However, an allegation of fraud “requires evidence which will pass a stiffer test …”: Balm at para 63; and see Balaz v James A Lewis Engineering, 1983 ABCA 90 at para 21; Mikisew Cree First Nation v Canada, 2002 ABCA 110 at para 61.
[25] A failure to provide enough evidence to meet the low evidentiary threshold supporting an amendment is sometimes characterized as a “hopeless” amendment: see comments in Attila at para 27.

However, the analysis is better understood as a failure to meet the evidentiary threshold for an amendment rather than engaging one of the exceptions. a)—Hopeless amendments [26] The exception for an impermissible or hopeless amendment involves a proposed pleading that, if in the original pleadings, would have been struck for suffering from one or more deficiencies identified in subrules 3.68(2) and
(3), which are summarized as follows: a.
The Court has no jurisdiction to hear the matter; b.
On the face of the proposed pleading, without resorting to evidence, the proposed pleading discloses no reasonable claim or defence to a claim; c.
The proposed pleading is frivolous, irrelevant or improper; d.
The proposed pleading constitutes an abuse of process; and e.
An irregularity in the proposed pleading is so prejudicial to the claim that it is sufficient to defeat the claim.

[27] In the normal course, the exception does not otherwise contemplate an inquiry into the merits of the allegation since a summary determination of the facts or questions of mixed fact and law is premature.
The pleadings define the scope of discovery and a summary adjudication of the merits usually occurs after each party has a reasonable opportunity to conduct discovery of records and witnesses.
Adjudicating the merits of a claim or defence without an adequate evidentiary foundation risks an unjust outcome.

[28] Some cases suggest that an amendment will be refused as hopeless where “it is clear that there is no genuine issue for trial, and the amended claim would not survive a summary judgment application”: CHS at para 11.
However, these authorities do not invite an adjudication of the merits before discovery nor treat the amendment application as a summary judgment (or dismissal) application.
The absence of an arguable claim or defence must be obvious.
The inability to resist summary judgment must be plain.
The possibility that discovery might alter the assessment of the merits should be considered.

[29] Even where discovery is already complete and the amendment will not re-open the discovery process, the logical sequencing is that the pleadings should be clarified before a summary adjudication occurs.

In this way, the claims and defences are clearly defined before the Court undertakes the modern approach to summary judgment in which consideration is given to whether the issues and interests involved lend themselves to a “proportionate, more expeditious and less expensive means to achieve a just result”: Hryniak v Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7 at para 4 [Hryniak].

[30] In Farm Credit, at para 17, the Alberta Court of Appeal confirmed that assessing the likely success of defences, determining whether a defence meets the civil burden of proof, and measuring amendments against the threshold for summary judgment is “usually inappropriate”.
Requiring more than a low measure of evidence risks converting an amendment application into a summary judgment application, which is contrary to all principle: Balm at para 29.
The pleadings should be settled before dealing with summary judgment: Elbow River Marketing v Canada Clean Fuels Inc, 2011 ABCA 258 at para 4.
In short, an amendment application is not a summary adjudication. b)—Bad faith amendments [31] The bad faith exception has received limited judicial interpretation.

However, the onus is on the party alleging bad faith to prove it on a balance of probabilities, not on the opposite party to disprove it: Hur v 726913 Alberta Ltd, 2013 ABQB 208 at paras 72, 76 [Hur].
[32] In the absence of something more, amending to defeat a summary judgment application does not demonstrate bad faith: Hur at para 73.

[33] In Hur, Justice Russell Brown (as he then was), at para 70, observed that “bad faith” has different meanings depending on the context, although the authorities provide little specific guidance about bad faith as the basis for refusing permission to amend pleadings.
He nevertheless found some assistance in comments from CS v MS, 2007 CanLII 20279, 38 RFL

(6th) 315 (Ont SCJ) at para 17, affirmed 2010 ONCA 196 [CS], which considered whether a party had engaged in “bad faith” under the costs provisions contained in Ontario's Family Law Rules, O Reg 114/99: In order to come within the meaning of bad faith in subrule 24(8), behaviour must be shown to be carried out with intent to inflict financial or emotional harm on the other party or other persons affected by the behaviour, to conceal information relevant to the issues or to deceive the other party or the court.

A misguided but genuine intent to achieve the ostensible goal of the activity, without proof of intent to inflict harm, to conceal relevant information or to deceive, saves the activity from being found to be in bad faith.
The requisite intent to harm, conceal or deceive does not have to be the person's sole or primary intent, but rather only a significant part of the person's intent.

At some point, a party could be found to be acting in bad faith when their litigation conduct has run the costs up so high that they must be taken to know their behaviour is causing the other party major financial harm without justification.
Stevenson and J.
Côté, Alberta Civil Procedure Handbook 2021, at 3-127, the editors state that when amending pleadings, bad faith seems to mean an intent to harm, to conceal or to deceive.
That interpretation effectively treats bad faith as a specific form of abuse of process arising after the original pleadings were filed.
Conversely, an abuse of process caused by the original pleadings is addressed by subrule 3.68(2)(d) and screened as a “hopeless” amendment.

[35] Based on the limited authorities, I conclude that the bad faith exception applies to proposed amendments that seek: a. to inflict financial or emotional harm on the adverse party or another person affected by the behaviour; b. to conceal information relevant and material to the litigation issues; or c. to deceive the adverse party or the Court.
[36] The exception is not to be used to punish negligent or careless delay that can be remedied through costs.
Moreover, the bad faith purpose need not be the applicant's sole or primary intent, so long as a significant feature of the intent was for an abuse of process to occur: CS at para 17.

[37] While past litigation conduct may be reviewed to deduce any improper purpose in seeking amendments, the inquiry should be conducted with specificity about how the prior conduct reveals an improper purpose in seeking the particular amendments.

A vague and sweeping approach to defining “bad faith” invites an overly expansive, complicated, and expensive application process that can obscure rather than reveal the motivations for specific amendments.
The exercise should not digress into sanctioning prior misconduct by denying amendments.

[38] Accordingly, an allegation of bad faith does not convert the pleading amendment process into a broad inquiry about the parties' past litigation conduct and the merits of proposed claims and defences, except where the exercise is truly necessary and compelling in showing that specific proposed amendments are motivated by an improper purpose.
Otherwise, even modest efforts to clarify issues for discovery and trial convert an interlocutory hearing into a complex and time-consuming exercise.
[39] The modern approach to litigation and the operation of the Rules favour timely and cost-effective procedures proportional to the remedy sought: Rule 1.2.

The Supreme Court of Canada in Hryniak recognized proportionality as a “touchstone for access to civil justice” and pressed for a culture shift by which judges are to “actively manage the legal process in line with the principle of proportionality”: paras 30 and 32.
The risk with an expanded inquiry is that bad faith will be alleged after any long delay and require a lengthy evidentiary record for a robust presentation of the merits.

An interlocutory application intended to clarify the issues instead swells and then swamps the proceedings. … [41] The amending process also should not be a preview or substitute for summary adjudication.
If the amendment has little or no merit, the opposing party can subsequently seek summary judgment with the advantage of a proper evidentiary record.
If the amendment was unnecessary, the additional expense can be addressed through costs, including enhanced costs.
[42] The doctrine of abuse of process is flexible and exists to ensure that the administration of justice is not brought into disrepute: Behn v Moulton Contracting Ltd, 2013 SCC 26 at para 41.
However, an allegation of bad faith in pursuing an amendment should rarely open the door to an elaborate review of the merits.
In Astolfi v.
Stone Creek Resorts Inc., 2023 ABKB 416, Justice Marion discussed when an amendment would not be allowed.

His Lordship said: [40] The most recent Alberta Court of Appeal framework provides that there is a strong presumption in favour of allowing amendments to pleadings after the close of pleadings: Kosteckyj v Paramount Resources Ltd, 2022 ABCA 230 at paras 12, 41
Pace v Economical Mutual Insurance, 2021 ABCA 1 at para 3
AARC Society v Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, 2019 ABCA 125 at para 85.
The applicant need not show any particular reason for needing the amendment: Attila Dogan Construction and Installation Co Inc v AMEC Americas Limited, 2014 ABCA 74 at para 24.

Courts should exercise their discretion to allow the amendment unless the non-moving party demonstrates an exception or compelling reason not to: Kosteckyj at paras 12, 41; Pace at para 3, 53; AARC Society at paras 6, 53.
[41] Courts must consider two distinct interests when assessing the merits of an amendment application:
(1) the impact the proposed amendment will have on the non-moving party's litigation interests; and

(2) the public interest in the resolution of litigation as quickly as reasonably possible without the expenditure of more public and private resources than is reasonably necessary: AARC Society at paras 57–62.
[42] What contemplates a compelling reason not to permit an amendment after the close of pleadings is not, and never has been, a closed list of exceptions.
However, while described in different ways by different courts, certain compelling reasons or grounds not to permit amendments have been recognized over time, including:

(a) the proposed amendment will significantly harm a legitimate litigation interest of the non-moving party; for example the proposed amendment will cause significant prejudice to a legitimate litigation interest of the non-moving party that cannot adequately be abridged by an ameliorative costs order or any other order: Pace at paras 4–5
Kosteckyj at para 41
AARC Society at para 64
Attila Dogan at para 25
Remington Development Corporation v Enmax Power Corporation, 2022 ABCA 71 at para 33

(b) the proposed amendment advances a claim that cannot possibly succeed or is hopeless because it would have been struck if it were in the original pleading; the test is whether it is plain and obvious that there is no triable issue: Swaleh v Lloyd, 2020 ABCA 18 at para 13

The Supreme Court has described a cause of action as “a set of facts that provides the basis for an action”: Markevich v Canada, 2003 SCC 9 (CanLII), 2003 SCC9 at para 27, [2003] 1 SCR 94 [Markevich] (emphasis added).

The presumptions and onus of proof in the two approaches are contra-posed.
The functional approach is characterised by the central question of whether the amendment will in fact prejudice the defendant in his/her defence of the action at trial.
It presumes the amendment should be granted unless the party opposing can show actual prejudice.
In contrast, the analytical approach presumes the amendment should not be granted unless the party seeking the amendment can show special circumstances.

So categorized, leave of the Court is required for Chenen to withdraw it.” At p.
8, Wilkins J. said: 48 The test for that leave is in my opinion correctly set forth in Edmonton (City) v.
Lovat Tunnel Equipment Inc., [2000] A.J.
No.
In that case, the Court concluded that a representation of counsel was tantamount to an amendment of the plaintiff's proceeding to withdraw a claim.
Justice Lee concluded that the test for leave to withdraw in relation to such a representation is the same as for a further amendment of a pleading to reassert that claim.

That is, it will be permitted where it can be made without prejudice to the opposite party which cannot be compensated in costs, there is no undue delay; and no limitation defence would be lost to the defendant.
Concurrent applications to amend and to strike In Hur v.
726913 Alberta Ltd., 2013 ABQB 208, Mr.

Justice Brown said: 27 Where an application for summary judgment is heard concurrently with a cross-application for permission to amend pleadings, the Court must determine the amendment application first before determining the application for summary judgment.
(Elbow River Marketing Limited Partnership v.
Canada Clean Fuels Inc., 2011 ABCA 258 at para.

3) It appears, from the face of Master Breitkreuz's order, that he followed this procedure, deferring consideration of summary judgment until the state of the pleadings had been determined: he first denied the Plaintiffs' application to amend the Statement of Claim, then summarily dismissed the Plaintiffs' claim against the Defendants.
An example of the application of this direction is found in Michael Awad Professional Corp. v.
531845 Alberta Inc., 2015 ABQB 296 (Master).
Master Robertson said: 14 Before oral arguments got underway, I drew to the attention of the parties Hur v.
726913 Alberta Ltd., 2013 ABQB 208 at para.

27, where the Court said that where there are cross-applications both for summary judgment and to amend the claim the court must hear and decide the application to amend before considering summary judgment.
Also, in Chevalier v.
Sunshine Village Corporation, 2011 ABQB 544, the Master allowed an application to amend to be brought before making his decision on an application to strike under Rule 3.68.
15 Accordingly, although the applications were argued together, it is incumbent upon the Court to decide the amendment application before deciding the application to strike.

16 It is not necessary for the defendant to bring a new application to strike; it is possible to deal with the application to strike taking into account the amended pleading, if in fact an amendment is allowed.
The Court must simply look at the proposed amended pleading instead of the original one to determine if it discloses a reasonable cause of action.
17 The application is made a little awkward by the fact that on an application to amend, there must be affidavit evidence filed in support to substantiate the need for the amendments.
In contrast, on an application to strike under Rule 3.68, the court is required to look only at the pleading and not at evidence.
Accordingly, I must consider the evidence that has been filed in support of the application to amend, but then ignore it for the application to strike.
